steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Voltage is the potential difference that drives charge through a circuit, measured in volts (V).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A); 1 A = 1 C/s.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Resistance opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Ohm's Law states V = IR, linking voltage, current and resistance linearly for ohmic conductors.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: A 12 V battery drives 3 A through a resistor. What is its resistance? | Q: What is the difference between conventional current and electron flow? | Q: A current of 2 A flows for 5 seconds. How much charge passes?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Using V = IR: R = V/I = 12/3 = 4 Ω. | Conventional current flows from positive to negative; electron flow is the actual movement of electrons from negative to positive. | Q = It = 2 × 5 = 10 C.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always state Ohm's Law as V = IR before rearranging in calculations. Show full working: write the formula, substitute values, then give the answer with units. Remember conventional current is positive to negative; exam questions often use this convention. Check that your answer is sensible: resistance should not be negative in basic circuits. When describing measurements, always specify whether the meter is in series (ammeter) or parallel (voltmeter).
